research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-23, first run, mode create, empty baseline, no research notes or prior evidence). 37 sources recorded, 36 opened. Read in full: Rolling Stone UK (S01), W (S02), Time Out 2023 (S03), the Guardian feature with Charrington, Chinouriri, Ward and Jesso Jr testimony (S04), ELLE 2026 cover (S10), ELLE 2025 Q&A (S11), NPR (S12), Numéro (S13, translated), the Music Week cover (S22) and the Braham interview (S23). YouTube captions transcribed and read: Zane Lowe (S15, 34 min), BBC Sidetracked (S16, 41 min), Apple Music One (S17, 27 min) and WSJ The One (S18, 12 min) in full; Bumble 2023 (S19, 32 min), the British Library panel (S20, 70 min, Dean's segments) and her drummer's podcast (S21, 92 min, the segments about her) searched by keyword and read around the hits. About 55,000 caption words in all. News and accuracy: S05-S09, S14, S24-S36. The 87-minute And The Writer Is... episode (S37) could not be transcribed (YouTube 429 / PO token). Evidence was gathered before choosing a type; the backlog's prior "Type 2" (2026-07-01 candidates list) was treated as a hypothesis only. Types tested: 2, 3, 7, 9, 6, and briefly 4 and 1. Outcome: status ready, profile_format standard, Type 2 at medium confidence, Type 3 the strongest alternative, Seven and Nine secondary. Not an open case: she has been public since 2018-19 and long-form interviews run from 2023, so the record is deep enough. The difficulty is that most of it is promotional and the testimony is friendly, not that it is young. Risks: contested_typing (several live rivals at medium confidence) and sensitive_allegations (the Withers-estate copyright suit; her disclosures about low mood, therapy and school exclusion), so the six-role jury applies.

Accuracy check (2026-10-23). The Art of Loving Live ended on 17 October 2026 at Western Springs Bowl, Auckland, after a nearly 40-minute sound failure; she apologized and played the full set (S32, S36). The Art of Loving was shortlisted for the 2026 Mercury Prize; RAYE won on 22 October 2026 (S33). The Mattie Music Group suit over "I've Seen It" was filed on 1 October 2026 against Capitol/UMG, Sony Music Publishing and Kobalt, with Dean not a defendant; no public response from her was found (S05). No third album has been announced; in April 2026 she said "I will make another album" (S14). "Rein Me In" became the longest-running UK No 1 on 31 July 2026 (S31). She told ELLE in February 2026 that she had deleted the social apps from her phone (S10); say exactly that, not "quit social media". A Manila Times report says she headlines LaLaLa Fest Manila on 14 January 2027; it was not opened, so do not print it unopened. 2027 Grammy nominations are pending: the backlog note predicting an Album of the Year nomination was not verified and must not be printed. Her relationship status is private; do not mention a partner (Wikipedia names one without a source we opened).

Drafting guidance (standard format). Strongest verified, durable hook: five days after winning Best New Artist, in a San Francisco hotel suite, she learns it is the ELLE writer's birthday and insists on giving her champagne: "Why are you here working?!" (S10, C15). Pair it with what she had just said onstage, that she is "a product of bravery", a phrase she already used about her grandmother at the British Library in July 2024 (S20, C31). Central question: is the warmth a giver's motive or a gifted professional's polish? Put Three beside Two near the type argument with its best evidence (C26, C07, C17); handle Seven (C23, C20) and Nine/Six (C11, C12) briefly but honestly. Present the independence and self-worth material (C19, C20, C35) as live tension, not as proof of "Two growth". Strong supporting details: the comfort-zone defence (C11); "I was always in someone else's space trying to prove something" (C10); her success definition, "how many people you can touch" (C14); the Ticketmaster sequence, apology first, then "BE BETTER" (C29); the Auckland apology at the tour finale (C30); "Carmen" as her proudest work and her word "selfish" for it (C40); the 2023 Mercury imposter line, "wangled my way in" (C09). Keep "## What is Olivia Dean's personality type?" with an answer of at most 60 words using "most likely"/"reads as" language at medium confidence, naming Three as the closest alternative. Target about 2,000-3,000 words. Mention the lawsuit, if at all, in one dated sentence ("allegation"; "not a defendant"; unresolved). Frontmatter: enneagram: 2; published: false; follow existing musician drafts for type (Olivia-Rodrigo.md uses ['musician', 'pop-star']); person slug olivia-dean. Possible internal links (check they are published): Sabrina-Carpenter, Chappell-Roan, sombr, Addison-Rae, Adele, Elton-John.

Quotation cautions. (a) S15-S21 are YouTube caption transcripts with unreliable speaker turns; check every printed quote against the audio at the locator, and do not tidy disfluencies into something she did not say. Zane Lowe supplied "you're an empath, right?"; Lowe is the Leo ("It's all about you unless it's all about me"), Dean the Pisces; "It's cool to show that you care" may be Lowe's. (b) In the Bumble podcast (S19), "it's just me and my dad" is the host; the "opinionated on other people's relationships" line has an unclear speaker, so do not use it. (c) Sidetracked (S16): "Christine" who made the tea is a colleague, not her mother. (d) ELLE 2025 (S11) lost its bold Q/A formatting; confirm "Every day is scary! I don't want to be scared." is Dean before quoting. (e) Numéro (S13) is translated: paraphrase, or mark it as translated. It also misdates "OK Love You Bye" (2021; correct is 2019) and calls her a "former singer" of Rudimental (she was a backing vocalist). (f) W (S02) also misdates "OK Love You Bye" to 2021. (g) The PA/ELLE UK quotes (S29) came through a page-reading tool; verify exact wording on the page before printing "I don't take any shit from people". (h) Grammy speech: "a granddaughter" (AP, RS UK body) vs "the granddaughter" (tweet, ELLE); check the broadcast. (i) Time Out calls her mother a barrister and ELLE a lawyer; use "lawyer". (j) BRIT entry age: 14, Year 10 (principal, S34), not 15 (Wikipedia). (k) Tour start: 22 vs 23 April 2026; write "April 2026". (l) The Ticketmaster refund statement says "real humans" (S28), not "real people". (m) ELLE writes "A Couple of Minutes"; the title is "A Couple Minutes". (n) "Here to please", "self-effacing and generous" and the scarf-knitting are the Time Out writer's words, not Dean's. The champagne gift is the ELLE writer's observation; attribute both. (o) Ward's comfort-zone quote is his recollection of her words (S04); attribute it as such.

Sensitivity. Mental health: in 2023 she described "quite a depressive state" and self-criticism before Messy, and she speaks openly about long-term therapy. Use these only in her words, dated, without diagnostic labels; never as type evidence on their own; never as the hook or the ending. School: she is reluctant to call it bullying ("I put it in a box"). Do not label it bullying in the author's voice, and do not build a causal childhood-wound story. Allegation: the Withers-estate suit is a civil complaint against her label and publishers; she is not a defendant; nothing is adjudicated. Do not imply copying, and do not let it colour the character argument. Privacy: do not name or discuss partners or dating rumours (a Harry Styles rumour circulated in 2025; she dismissed it), her brother, or her grandmother's health beyond "unwell" as Dean put it. Race and identity: quote her own words on being mixed-race and "other"; avoid author-voice generalizations. Politics: the Grammy speech line is about her grandmother and immigrants; report it in her words and do not frame her as a political campaigner.

Follow-ups for the next refresh: (1) transcribe the 87-minute And The Writer Is... episode (S37; YouTube yzWbab28z38) via audio and whisper, for private-process and conflict material; (2) find the WSJ Magazine print profile (quoted secondhand as "I was terrible" about her Rudimental job) and the Evening Standard 2024 interview (inkl excerpt truncated); (3) look for any on-record words from her mother, her aunt or Emily Braham about what she is like when things go wrong; (4) listen to S15 at 06:30-10:45, 17:15-18:20 and 31:30-32:40, S16 at 06:00-09:45, and S19 at 10:00-12:50 to confirm wording and speakers; (5) watch for her first long interview after the tour and the 2027 Grammy nominations: when she describes what she most wants from the next record and life off the road, does she talk about people and giving (Two), goals and standing (Three), freedom and new experiences (Seven), or peace and comfort (Nine)? (6) Track the lawsuit docket and any response; (7) check whether she returns to personal social media.

sources.title: The art of Olivia Dean
sources.speaker: Olivia Dean, interviewed by phone from her south London home by Rolling Stone UK (byline not shown on page)
sources.date: 2025-09-01 (August/September 2025 print issue; spoken shortly after her Sam Fender stadium supports and before the 26 September album release)
sources.locator: Paragraph 3 ("I love playing shows so much" / "makes me feel most useful"); paragraph 9 (Carmen, shared bedroom, "I'm very close with my granny"); paragraph 13 (karate, mum: "Pack it in, babe"); paragraphs 15-17 (Mr Doherty and Paul Simon; Rudimental; "I'm a real observer"); paragraph 18 (studio anxiety, "trying to justify myself"); paragraphs 21-22 (Mickalene Thomas, bell hooks, "how to fill each other with care"); paragraph 28 ("Oh, I think I'm quite great") | Edit stage (2026-10-23): Rudimental paragraphs; "odd one out" paragraph; cover-art paragraph.
sources.excerpt: “I love playing shows so much,” she enthuses, a reassuring statement from someone who will play no less than four shows at London’s O2 Arena next spring. “It’s the thing that makes me feel most useful in my life, and it’s something that I really love to do. I don’t really get nervous. I just get intensely excited. It’s all about being with people. While I love to sing personally, for myself, I find shows are the closest thing to this… it sounds kind of cliche, but… spirituality. I just feel it’s such a powerful thing.” [...] “I’m very close with my granny,” Dean explains. “She was very present when I was growing up, and at one point, we were roomies — we shared a bedroom. When I was writing [Messy], she wasn’t doing so well, and we were spending a lot of time together, and I was asking her lots of questions about her life. She was telling me about coming to this country when she was 18. I thought, ‘Oh gosh, I don’t know if I could have done that: arriving somewhere and just being like, ‘OK, let’s find a job, and find somewhere to live.’ She had four kids by the time she was my age, which is crazy. She made a life for herself with the foresight that she wanted the life of her children, and their children, to be a better one. [...] “She was like, ‘Pack it in, babe, choose a hobby — you’re doing too much,’” Dean laughs. [...] I’m a real observer, I think, and I like to learn, and then apply,” she says, “without sounding too clinical about it.” [...] “I had developed a bit of studio anxiety, I suppose, and was putting a lot of pressure on myself,” she explains. “I realised that all this time that I’ve been making music, I’ve never had my own studio. I’ve always been coming into other people’s spaces and trying to justify myself. | Edit stage additions: "you get the opportunity to play in front of those big crowds, but it's not about you — you can learn and take that feeling in, without the pressure"; "OK, could I do this myself?"; "a little bit like the odd one out"; "It's representative of imperfection... it's just my truth. I kind of want people to hear their own truth"; "For that performance, her first time playing the festival" (contradicted by S03/S22).
sources.context: Long magazine profile with extended first-person quotation. Promotional context (second-album launch); the writer frames the material. Mother described here as former deputy leader of the Women's Equality Party. Further quotes used in claims: "how to fill each other with care" and the So Easy explanation ("Why shouldn't somebody want to fall in love with you?"). Draft stage: also used for the blurred album covers ("I kind of want people to hear their own truth"), the photos and piano brought to the east London house, and Carmen's photo on her chest at Glastonbury.

sources.title: Olivia Dean Makes Space for Herself With New Album ‘The Art of Loving’
sources.speaker: Olivia Dean, Zoom interview with Cat Cardenas (W Magazine)
sources.locator: Paragraphs 2-5 (LA sessions, "If I did it the first time...", "I was always in someone else's space trying to prove something"); paragraphs 10-14 (hooks, dating culture, parents together almost 30 years, "Perhaps that's why I'm such a romantic", "My mum and my auntie and my granny are too powerful"); paragraph 15 ("romantic love isn't the be-all and end-all")
sources.excerpt: “I just thought, If I did it the first time and I didn’t know what I was doing, can I do it again?” [...] “I was always in someone else’s space trying to prove something,” she says. “[Now I had] this control and trust in myself and what I was making that I’d never experienced before.” [...] “Perhaps that’s why I’m such a romantic,” she says. [...] “It would have been impossible for me to not have developed into the feminist I identify as today because of them,” she says. “My mum and my auntie and my granny are too powerful. At the same time, there’s room for both: you can be this independent, strong woman and still have love. I don’t think they’re mutually exclusive.” [...] “I’ve only become more crystallized in the sense that romantic love isn’t the be-all and end-all of my life,” she says. “When you’re younger, you’re led to believe that it is, but I feel love in so many areas of my life.”
sources.context: Short feature built on one Zoom interview. Error: the page dates "OK Love You Bye" to 2021; it was released in 2019 (S35). Do not copy that date.

sources.title: Olivia Dean: ‘It’s easy to let other people tell you what you should be doing’ (page title: ‘It’s hard to see myself as part of it, sometimes’)
sources.speaker: Olivia Dean, interviewed in person in Dalston by Chiara Wilkinson (Time Out London); writer's observations
sources.date: 2023-11-13 (interview mid-October 2023, after the Messy release and Mercury shortlist)
sources.locator: Opening paragraphs (writer: "so self-effacing and generous"); Highams Park paragraph ("I didn't love growing up there"); fame paragraph ("my ambition is not to be famous"); Goldsmiths paragraph ("I'm not cringe!", "I learned that I had to be selfish"); Messy paragraph ("My heart has got a hard case"); Mercury paragraph ("wangled my way in"; "very self-critical"; "quite a depressive state"; therapy); pub paragraph (writer: "She's here to please"; knits scarves for her mum); closing quotes ("pretty positive person"; "I pride myself on being a good person"; "best show I've ever seen"; "I feel like a mess of things") | Edit stage (2026-10-23): Highams Park paragraph; Goldsmiths paragraph; Chanel paragraph; pub paragraph; heritage paragraph.
sources.excerpt: It’s not often you come across someone so confident in themselves, so bubbly and yet so self-effacing and generous. [...] ‘I didn’t love growing up there,’ she says, a pitch higher. ‘I felt quite different to everybody else. In primary school, I was one of the only Black girls. I think that’s what made me want to get out and go to BRIT [school].’ [...] ‘I was like, oh, they’ve just had to fill a space,’ she says, somewhat earnestly. ‘They just probably whacked me on the side. I’ve just wangled my way in. [...] ‘There was a big chunk of time where I was in a pattern of being very self-critical – to the point where you just feel so shit about yourself, comparing your beginning point to everyone else's finished product,’ she says. ‘That is just the thief of joy. I was honestly in quite a depressive state. I got out of it: I’ve been doing therapy and learning how I function and what environment I function best in. Therapy is awesome. [...] She smiles, flirts, makes sarcastic jokes and never breaks eye contact. She’s here to please. [...] ‘Honestly, I think I’m just a pretty positive person,’ she says. ‘I’m definitely, like, not bubbly and happy all the time. But I feel like I’m very lucky in my life right now and I have a lot to be grateful for. I pride myself on being a good person, because nobody wants to work with a horrible person. It’s not a productive way to move through the industry.’ | Edit stage additions: "I felt quite different to everybody else. In primary school, I was one of the only Black girls."; "it felt like you had to be making something really alternative and left to be cool [there]"; "I learned that I know best, which can sound dickheaded... Who gives a fuck what other people think about it?"; "You kind of don't have a choice... It's the same with fashion as it is with music."; "She smiles, flirts, makes sarcastic jokes and never breaks eye contact. She's here to please."; "instead of being negative, which it was for me when I was younger, I'm trying to make it a positive."; "She played her first Glastonbury show."
sources.context: The fullest pre-breakthrough portrait (age 24). The "here to please", "generous" and scarf-knitting details are the writer's observations and characterizations, not quotes. Time Out calls her mother "a barrister"; ELLE (S10) says lawyer in child and family law. Mental-health content ("quite a depressive state", therapy) is her own account; handle per sensitivity guidance. Also contains: "If I stay in this environment I'll start to believe that I'm cringe – and I'm not cringe!" and "I learned that I had to be selfish. And make myself happy first." Draft-stage correction: "I learned that I had to be selfish. And make myself happy first." is said about creative decisions on Messy (it follows "I learned that I know best" and "It's very easy to let other people tell you what you should be doing"), not about love; the draft uses it in that context (C44). The ceremony line "When I got to the actual award show, I was like, no, I'm supposed to be here" follows the "wangled" passage and is quoted with it. The writer notes the interview ran "longer than expected" in the pub.

sources.title: Hard work, romance and bell hooks: how Olivia Dean became British pop’s newest megastar
sources.speaker: Shaad D'Souza (Guardian), quoting Jo Charrington (president, Capitol Records UK), Rachel Chinouriri (BRIT School classmate and musician), Willem Ward (Capitol A&R) and Tobias Jesso Jr (co-writer of Man I Need)
sources.locator: Paragraph 6 (Grammy speech quote); paragraph 7 (Charrington: "super intentional"); paragraph 8 (Chinouriri: "is such a light"); paragraph 11 (Ward: "intentional with everything she does"; comfort-zone quote); paragraph 12 (Hackney house, producers she felt most comfortable with); paragraph 13 (Jesso Jr); paragraph 14 (Charrington: "she works bloody hard")
sources.excerpt: Jo Charrington, president of Dean’s label Capitol Records UK, says that Dean is “super intentional about what kind of records she wants to make – and that’s not common”. Charrington says that some artists she works with have an unfocused process, and “will want to write, like, 200 songs, and we’ll get 10. For Olivia, once she had an idea of the record she wanted to make, she would go, ‘This is the timeframe I want to do it in, let’s do it.’ And you just believe her – it’s real confidence.” [...] Dean herself “is such a light. You can tell she really wants the best for herself and to extend that to everyone who surrounds her”. [...] “One of the first things she said was, ‘Sometimes, the saying get outside of your comfort zone is confusing to me, because I really want to be in my comfort zone.’” [...] She was very sure of what she did and did not like, which made the process very easy for both of us. [...] “And it’s a lot of hard work. I will say: she works bloody hard.”
sources.context: The only reported piece built on named testimony from people who work closely with her. All four speakers have professional or friendly incentives to praise her (label president, A&R, co-writer, close friend and peer), and the piece ran the day of the Brits. Ward's comfort-zone line is his recollection of something she said. Note: this piece says she entered the BRIT School at 15; the principal (S34) says 14. The draft does not state an entry age.

sources.title: Olivia Dean accused of plagiarism on her I’ve Seen It track
sources.speaker: Ramon Antonio Vargas (Guardian), quoting the Mattie Music Group complaint
sources.date: 2026-10-02 (suit filed Thursday 1 October 2026, US federal court, Los Angeles)
sources.locator: Whole article: plaintiff, claim, defendants (Sony Music Publishing, Capitol/UMG, Kobalt), Dean and co-writers not named as defendants, 17 August notice, no immediate response from Dean's representatives
sources.excerpt: Mattie Music Group contended that Dean’s track I’ve Seen It stole “substantial” aspects of Withers’ 1981 collaboration with Grover Washington Jr, which ascended to No 2 on Billboard’s Hot 100 before enjoying a comeback much more recently on the TikTok social media platform. [...] The lawsuit does not list as defendants Dean or her I’ve Seen It collaborators, Bastian Langbaek and Max Wolfgang. But the lawsuit alleges the three “had a reasonable opportunity to encounter the original work before creating I’ve Seen It”, the last track on Dean’s 2025 album The Art of Loving. [...] Representatives for Dean, Capitol Records and Kobalt did not immediately respond to requests for comment from the Guardian on Friday. Billboard reported that a Kobalt representative declined to comment on the lawsuit.
sources.context: An allegation in a civil complaint, unresolved as of 2026-10-23. Dean is not a defendant. Report only as an allegation, with the defendants' lack of public response, and do not characterize the song as copied.

sources.title: Olivia Dean review – a powerful, affirming night with a pop star at the height of her powers
sources.speaker: Brodie Lancaster (Guardian), reviewing the Rod Laver Arena, Melbourne show and paraphrasing/quoting Dean's onstage remarks
sources.date: 2026-10-06 (show: first Melbourne night of the Australia/New Zealand leg, early October 2026)
sources.locator: Paragraphs 5-7 (credits; onstage hooks paraphrase; "realise that [she] deserve[s] that too"; Let Alone the One You Love lyric)
sources.excerpt: “This album was about me trying to understand what love really means to me,” Dean tells the crowd in Melbourne, paraphrasing a passage from hooks: to love another person is to want them to be the best version of themselves. Love them outside of who they are to you, she urges the crowd. [...] Giving that gift to a lover made her “realise that [she] deserve[s] that too”. The keys kick in for Let Alone the One You Love, the song Dean says she wrote the moment that idea clicked: “If you knew me at all / You wouldn’t try to keep me small / You wouldn’t do that to a friend / Let alone the one you love.”
sources.context: Concert review; the onstage remarks are partly paraphrased by the critic (only the bracketed fragments are quotation). Observation of how she frames the album to a 14,000-capacity crowd near the end of the tour.

sources.title: Olivia Dean defends immigrants during Grammys speech
sources.speaker: Olivia Dean (Grammy acceptance speech, 1 February 2026), as transcribed by Rolling Stone UK
sources.locator: Paragraphs 2-3 (speech quotes, including thanks to manager Emily, "We've been doing this for 10 years"); paragraph 5 (closing line); embedded tweet uses "the granddaughter" | Edit stage (2026-10-23): Paragraph 2.
sources.excerpt: “For me, I never really imagined that I would be up here, let alone nominated,” Dean said smiling in a sparkly black dress. claims.claim: ELLE's Sylvia Obell, interviewing Dean in her St. Regis suite in San Francisco on Friday 6 February 2026, five days after the Grammys, wrote that on learning it was Obell's birthday Dean insisted on giving her a bottle of Veuve Clicquot: "Why are you here working?!"
claims.passage: Obell wrote that Dean insisted on giving her a bottle of Veuve Clicquot champagne. "Why are you here working?!" Dean exclaimed.
claims.inference: The champagne gift is the clearest unprompted act on record: attention instantly redirected to the other person's day, five days after her own Grammy. It matches the Time Out writer's observation in 2023 under very different career conditions.
claims.alternative: Hospitality toward a cover-story writer is also good press practice, and both writers were charmed fans. "She's here to please" is the writer's interpretation. Two anecdotes are a pattern hint, not proof.

claims.claim: Obell replied: "Uh, do you know who you are?! You just won a Grammy!"
claims.passage: Obell shot back: "Uh, do you know who you are?! You just won a Grammy!"
claims.inference: The writer's own retort frames the inversion the opening relies on: the Grammy winner turning attention to the writer.
claims.alternative: The exchange is reported by an openly admiring writer in a cover story; it is one scene.

claims.claim: Dean had been lighting candles before the interview and said "I like to set a vibe"; the interview took place a few hours before she headlined a Super Bowl kickoff party, on Friday 6 February 2026, five days after the Grammys.
claims.passage: "I like to set a vibe," she told the writer who walked in
claims.inference: Hosting detail observed by the writer; sets the scene and dates the interview (Super Bowl LX weekend; the Grammys were 1 February).
claims.alternative: Ordinary hospitality for a cover shoot; scene-setting, not motive evidence.

claims.claim: The ELLE interview was on Friday 6 February 2026, hours before her Super Bowl party headline set.
claims.passage: It was Friday, February 6, 2026, a few hours before Dean headlined a Super Bowl party.
claims.inference: ELLE says it was the Friday of Super Bowl weekend, five days after the Grammy, a few hours before her performance at an Uber-hosted kickoff party where she was the headliner.
claims.alternative: Date inferred from "Super Bowl weekend... this particular Friday night" and "five days since" the 1 February Grammys.

claims.claim: The ELLE writer framed the champagne gift as Dean romanticizing ordinary moments; the recipient was writing her cover story.
claims.passage: Obell read it as style: Dean, she wrote, "romanticizes life the way she makes music." It was also a kindness to the writer of her cover story. Both readings stay open.
claims.inference: Gives the hook's rival readings next to it (critic-04): an aesthetic habit, and generosity toward the person shaping her press image.
claims.alternative: Neither reading is established; a giver could be both stylish and press-aware.

claims.claim: Accepting Best New Artist on 1 February 2026, she spoke as the granddaughter of an immigrant: "I'm a product of bravery, and I think those people deserve to be celebrated." Her grandmother came to Britain from Guyana alone at 18.
claims.passage: She turned her Grammy speech toward her grandmother, who came to Britain from Guyana alone at 18, and toward immigrants like her.
claims.inference: The speech turned the moment toward her grandmother, immigrants and her team; the "product of bravery" phrase was already hers at the British Library in July 2024 (S20).
claims.alternative: Outlets differ on "a" or "the granddaughter"; check the broadcast. The speech came amid US immigration politics (ICE protest pins in the audience), so it was also a public stance. Do not overstate it as a political campaign.

claims.claim: Playing live is "the thing that makes me feel most useful in my life... It's all about being with people" (RS UK, interview published September 2025).
claims.passage: "It's the thing that makes me feel most useful in my life."
claims.inference: Purpose and success answers given to two different writers (Rolling Stone UK, interview published September 2025; ELLE, February 2026) use usefulness, helping and touching people as her own terms (C14, C14c, C14d). This is the most direct motive-language for a Two reading. The Apple Music "something to give" line (C14h) answered a question about talent, not purpose, and is not counted here (verify-01).
claims.alternative: The album campaign rewards love-and-connection answers, and "connection" is standard artist language. A Three can sincerely define success by reach, and "how many people you can gather" is also a ticket count. Treat this as self-presentation that the observed behaviour (C15, C29, C30) must corroborate.

claims.claim: Same RS UK answer: "It's all about being with people."

claims.passage: "My purpose in music is to help people, myself included, find compassion and a deeper connection with one another."

claims.claim: Asked how she knew her talent was special, she said she was never competitive and always knew she had something to give.
claims.passage: she said, "I've never felt like a competitive nature," and, "I always knew that I had something to give."
claims.inference: Apple Music (Oct 2025), 06:09-06:40; captions and a second machine transcription agree on both lines. Asked how she knew her talent was special, she answered with non-competition and the sense that "there's space for everybody... everyone has so much to bring to the table", so "something to give" means having something to bring alongside her peers. The article frames it that way and does not count it as a purpose answer or in the Two-versus-Three discriminator (verify-01). At most weak anti-Three self-report.
claims.alternative: Campaign-era self-report; in Time Out 2023 she described comparing herself to others while making Messy, so "never competitive" is her current self-description, not an observed fact.

claims.claim: Article caveat: these are campaign answers; words need behaviour behind them.

claims.inference: States the limit from C14's alternative.

claims.claim: Her 21 November 2025 Instagram statement opened with an apology to fans and a note that her team was looking into it.
claims.passage: Her Instagram statement that day opened with an apology. "I'm sorry that there seems to be an issue with ticket re-selling and pricing," she wrote. "My team are currently looking into it." She added that "the last thing I want is for anyone to be scammed or overcharged for our show."
claims.inference: Described as one statement that opened with an apology, not as separate stories (subject-F2): THR says "Dean wrote on an Instagram story"; Variety says "She continued". The omitted "My team are currently looking into it" is restored.
claims.alternative: Apology-then-blame is ordinary artist crisis messaging (C29g).

claims.claim: Resale listings marked up by hundreds of dollars appeared within hours of the 21 November 2025 on-sale.
claims.passage: On November 21, 2025, tickets for the North American leg of her Art of Loving Live tour went on general sale. Within hours fans were posting screenshots of resale listings marked up by hundreds of dollars
claims.inference: Names the tour once and places the November sale on its North American leg (unfamiliar-04, future-04): Variety says general tickets went on sale that morning after the tour announcement; S36 lists the US/Canada dates as her first arena headlining there; PA says the cap applied to "the North American run of the tour".
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Her second post, as Variety Australia transcribed it.
claims.passage: "@ticketmaster @livenation @aegpresents you are providing a disgusting service. The prices at which you're allowing tickets to be re-sold is vile and completely against our wishes. Live music should be affordable and accessible... BE BETTER."
claims.inference: Variety: "She continued," after the apology; THR independently transcribes the same wording. The ellipsis omits "and we need to find a new way of making that possible."
claims.alternative: Image-positive stand; artists often have some control over resale (C29f).

claims.claim: On 27 November 2025 she announced refunds of the difference above face value and said every artist and team should be able to cap resale before the on-sale.
claims.passage: On November 27 she announced that Ticketmaster and AXS would refund the difference to anyone who had paid over face value. "Every artist and their team should be granted the option to cap re-sale at face value ahead of on sale," she wrote
claims.inference: PA quotes her statement: "Ticketmaster and AXS have agreed to refund the difference to anyone who has paid over face value" and "Every artist and their team should be granted the option to cap re-sale at face value ahead of on sale". Her published answer on the resale-control question (subject-F1).
claims.alternative: Her statement does not say what her team had chosen before the sale.

claims.claim: She said the industry has a responsibility to protect people and community.
claims.passage: and "we as an industry have a responsibility to protect people and our community."
claims.alternative: Public statement; also good PR.

claims.claim: Live Nation's CEO endorsed her call.
claims.passage: Live Nation's chief executive, Michael Rapino, said the company would "echo Olivia's call to do better."
claims.inference: PA: Rapino: "we echo Olivia's call to do better and have taken steps to lead by example." Shows the companies sided with her within a week (critic-03).
claims.alternative: Corporate statements are positioning; the UK had just announced a face-value resale ban that Ticketmaster backed (S27).

claims.claim: No opened source says what her team's resale settings were before the sale.
claims.passage: No source opened for this profile says what her team's resale settings were.
claims.inference: THR: "At press time, it's unclear what Dean's team's policy was." Neither Variety nor PA reports it. The question is left visibly open (subject-F1).
claims.alternative: A later report could settle it either way.
claims.review_trigger: If a source reports the resale settings her team chose before the 21 November 2025 on-sale, state them here and in the Ticketmaster FAQ.

claims.claim: Counterpoint: THR noted artists often have some control over resale policy and her own team's policy was unclear.
claims.passage: The Hollywood Reporter noted that artists often have some control over resale policy and that it was unclear what her own team's policy had been.
claims.inference: THR: "artists often exert some level of control of their resale policies"; "it's unclear what Dean's team's policy was".
claims.alternative: None; this is the counterpoint.

claims.claim: Within one statement, the apology to fans came before the complaint; this is weak evidence.
claims.passage: The order is the detail, though a small one: her statement put the fans before the complaint. Apology-then-remedy is also how any well-run artist team handles a bad on-sale.
claims.inference: Interpretation with its limit stated (subject-F2, critic-03, enneagram-2): order inside a single post is thin evidence, and apology-then-remedy is the standard crisis script.
claims.alternative: Standard artist crisis communication; does not separate Two from Three.

claims.claim: The call-out cost her little because the companies backed her within a week; a Three could do the same.
claims.passage: The companies backed her within a week, so it cost her little. A Three could make the same move.
claims.inference: Ticketmaster capped resale the same day (S26); Live Nation endorsed her call on 27 Nov (S28). Replaces the "fight" framing (critic-03).
claims.alternative: She could not know in advance that they would back her; the risk at posting time was real but small.

claims.claim: Ticketmaster replied the same day, capping resale on its site and saying it supports artists' ability to set resale terms.
claims.passage: Ticketmaster answered within hours, reposting her message, capping resale on its site at face value and adding, "We support artists' ability to set the terms of how their tickets are sold and resold." That put the question back on her side.
claims.inference: Variety: Ticketmaster reposted her message and added "We support artists' ability to set the terms of how their tickets are sold and resold. @oliviadeano, we will cap resale prices on our site at face value". Gives the company's reply (subject-F1, critic-03).
claims.alternative: The reply can be read as deflection or as fair comment; the article leaves it unresolved (C29m).

claims.claim: FAQ: the Ticketmaster sequence and outcome.
claims.passage: On November 21, 2025, tickets for the North American leg of her Art of Loving Live tour showed up on resale sites at inflated prices. Her Instagram statement opened with an apology to fans, then told Ticketmaster, Live Nation and AEG they were "providing a disgusting service" and to "BE BETTER."
claims.inference: FAQ restates the single statement, not separate stories (subject-F2).
claims.alternative: As C29.

claims.claim: FAQ: Ticketmaster's reply, the refunds and her call for artist resale caps.
claims.passage: Ticketmaster replied that it supports artists' ability to set resale terms and capped resale on its site at face value. On November 27 she announced that Ticketmaster and AXS would refund the difference to anyone who had paid over face value, and said every artist should get the option to cap resale at face value before tickets go on sale.
claims.inference: Paraphrases S26 and S28 for the FAQ.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Her firm hold on her own agenda tells against Nine.
claims.passage: Nine's problem is how firmly she holds her own agenda: "it's got to be my story," "I need to be across all of it," and a manager who says "she is across everything."
claims.inference: Discriminator against Nine (enneagram-7): her own words on authorship (S16, S15) and Braham's "she is across everything", said of a 50/50 business partnership (S23). The Ticketmaster post is no longer used against Nine, and "very stubborn" is no longer leaned on here, since Braham pairs it with "open to learning" (verify-05).
claims.alternative: A Nine can be firm about a few things; the evidence is about her work only, and Braham also says they often come round to each other's viewpoint.

claims.claim: Each rival explains a piece; Two also explains her purpose answers.
claims.passage: Each rival explains a piece: Three the drive and the polish, Seven the joy and the freedom, Four the authorship and the sad songs, Nine the peace. Only Two also explains the purpose answers.
claims.inference: Summary of the type comparison; points back to C51g instead of restating it (verify-06).
claims.alternative: Rests on self-report (C51c).

claims.claim: At the final show of the tour (Western Springs Bowl, Auckland, 17 October 2026, about 40,000 people), sound failure halted the concert for almost 40 minutes. She returned and said: "I'm so sorry about that, everybody. That's never happened before... We're not going to cut anything, we're going to give you what you paid for."
claims.passage: "I'm so sorry about that, everybody," she told the crowd when she came back, and then promised: "We're not going to cut anything, we're going to give you what you paid for."
claims.inference: Under public stress her reflex is apology and making it right for the audience, consistent with the ticketing episode (C29).
claims.alternative: Ordinary professional conduct for a headliner; the promoter confirmed the full show. Weak evidence alone; useful only as a pattern with C29.

claims.claim: Auckland, 17 October 2026, final night of the tour: a sound failure stopped the show after three songs for nearly 40 minutes.
claims.passage: On October 17, 2026, at Western Springs Bowl in Auckland, the last night of the Art of Loving Live tour, a sound failure stopped the show after three songs for nearly 40 minutes
claims.inference: 1News: "to conclude her Art of Loving Live tour"; the tour is named (unfamiliar-04, future-04).
claims.alternative: Promoter attributed the fault to tour production.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the sequence matches November (sorry first, then making it right).
claims.passage: Any headliner apologizes after a 40-minute stoppage. Auckland matches November only in direction: sorry first, then making it right for the people in front of her.
claims.inference: Self-limiting: Auckland is not presented as an established pattern on its own (subject-F2, enneagram-2).
claims.alternative: Standard service recovery; it does not separate any types.

claims.claim: Rachel Chinouriri, a BRIT School classmate and musician, told the Guardian (February 2026) that Dean "is such a light. You can tell she really wants the best for herself and to extend that to everyone who surrounds her."
claims.passage: Dean "is such a light. You can tell she really wants the best for herself and to extend that to everyone who surrounds her."
claims.inference: Independent voices (friend, peer artist, band member) in different outlets agree on warmth that extends to others, and Chinouriri was praising her as early as 2023 (S25).
claims.alternative: All are friends or colleagues speaking in promotional contexts; no critical or intimate family testimony exists. Warmth is compatible with Seven or Nine sociability as well as with Two.

claims.claim: Chinouriri is a BRIT School classmate and friend, now a musician.
claims.passage: Rachel Chinouriri, a BRIT School classmate and friend who is now a musician herself
claims.inference: Guardian: "Dean's Brit school classmate Rachel Chinouriri, a successful musician in her own right"; The Forty-Five (2023) interviews them together as friends. Corrects "People who work with her" (fan-08).
claims.alternative: A friend's testimony.

claims.claim: Her drummer Joel Waters said on a 2026 podcast he could talk to someone in the band, "or I can even speak to Olivia", about trouble at home.
claims.passage: that if things were hard at home he could talk to someone in the band, "or I can even speak to Olivia."
claims.inference: A general remark about friendship in the band; captions and whisper agree.
claims.alternative: Not a specific incident; a band member with a stake in the act.

claims.claim: Joel Waters has toured as her drummer for about seven years (his account, May 2026).
claims.passage: Joel Waters, her touring drummer, said on a [2026 podcast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=luX3FbprMG0) that he had been on the road with her for seven years
claims.inference: S21 (2026): "I've been on the road for the last 7 years with a singer called Olivia Dean." Duration anchored to the 2026 source (future-02).
claims.alternative: The Time Out writer frames the truck tour as "to cheer up strangers"; that motive is the writer's, not Dean's. The truck tour was brand-sponsored (Clarks, per Wikipedia), so it was also a marketing solution.
claims.review_trigger: If Dean changes manager, label or touring band, update the role labels.

claims.claim: Time Out's Chiara Wilkinson (2023) found her "so self-effacing and generous" and wrote "She's here to please"; these are the writer's words.
claims.passage: Time Out's Chiara Wilkinson found her "so self-effacing and generous." After their interview ran long in a pub, Wilkinson wrote that Dean "smiles, flirts, makes sarcastic jokes and never breaks eye contact. She's here to please." Those are the writer's words, not Dean's, and they describe charm as much as giving.
claims.inference: Time Out 2023: "She smiles, flirts, makes sarcastic jokes and never breaks eye contact. She's here to please." Restores the sentence's context (fan-02); no longer offered as giving evidence.
claims.alternative: The writer's impression in a warm profile.

claims.claim: After the 2026 Grammy discourse she said you cannot please everybody and she has peace in that.
claims.passage: Dean's own words, after her 2026 Grammy, ran the other way: "You can't please everybody. And I have such peace in that," she told ELLE.
claims.inference: ELLE 2026, on online discourse after the Grammys: "I know who I am... You can't please everybody. And I have such peace in that." Direct counterevidence to a people-pleasing reading (fan-02, enneagram-3).
claims.alternative: Said after years of therapy and in the week of maximum approval; also the Nine's best line (C12b).

claims.claim: At 17, at her first coffee with Emily Braham, Dean listed three goals (Later... with Jools Holland, an album, Glastonbury), all achieved by 2024 (Later... TV debut and Messy in 2023, Glastonbury 2024).
claims.passage: At 17, at her first coffee with Emily Braham, who was still managing her in 2026, Dean listed three goals: play _Later... with Jools Holland_, make an album, and play Glastonbury.
claims.inference: Manager status dated to 2026 (future-02): S08 Grammy speech and S23 Music Week (2026).
claims.alternative: A clear, early, finite goal list fits Three-style achievement orientation as much as anything relational. Report the story; do not over-read it.

claims.claim: Apple Music, October 2025: "That was all I wanted to do"; she has had to "think of some new goals."
claims.passage: "That was all I wanted to do," she said on Apple Music in October 2025. By 2024 she had done all three and had to "think of some new goals."
claims.inference: Glastonbury: Music Week (S22) dates her first set to 2023 (Lonely Hearts Club stage, "two years ago" in Sept 2025) and the Pyramid Stage to 2024; Messy released 2023. "By 2024" holds either way.
claims.alternative: A finite early goal list fits Three; also simply ambition.

claims.claim: In 2025 she named headlining Glastonbury as a new goal.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) Independence and self-protection: "I also can really function alone" (C20), "intensely romantic, but also no worries if not" (C20c), "I'm too scared to belong to anyone", a restatement of her own "Something Inbetween" lyric (C20d, C20e), "My heart has got a hard case" (C20b). (2) Approval independence, which strains every heart-type reading: after the February 2026 Grammys she deleted the apps because "I don't think you're supposed to know everyone's opinion about you" (C25), "You can't please everybody. And I have such peace in that" (C47); and in 2023 the defiant "I learned that I had to be selfish... Who gives a fuck what other people think" (C44). (3) Tight control of her work: no features, "I need to be across all of it", a manager who says both are "very stubborn" (C35, C35b, C35c). (4) The Two behaviour is low-cost, audience-rewarded or conventional: a gift to her cover writer (C15f), acceptance speeches (C49f), apology-then-remedy twice (C29g, C30c); the companies backed her within a week (C29n). (5) Much of the Two material is promotional love-talk (C14f), the testimony is friendly (C16c), the pre-2023 record is thin (C16e), and therapy vocabulary shapes her self-analysis (C42b). (6) No Two shadow behaviour appears: no over-giving, martyrdom or resentment at being unappreciated (C54).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Three explains the drive and the polish. She set a three-goal list with her manager at 17 and completed it by 2024 (C07, C07b), and in 2025 wanted to headline Glastonbury (C07d). She wants audiences to call it "the best show I've ever seen" (C26c); what she was "too much" for at school was "wanting to shine" (C24d, C46). She carries her mother's "five times better" standard (C02), though ELLE sets it beside her mother's feminist political career and it may describe an unequal bar (C02c, C02d). Her label stresses her work ethic (C26); she manages her image (Chanel, stage clothes as "this elevated version of myself", C26d); she justifies goodness instrumentally (C17). Three shares the heart centre, so the worth language (C24) does not separate Two from Three. Her candor about failure (Messy, "wangled", the LA sessions, the charts) was told from success and fits a Three comeback story (C51e, C51f). What strains Three: when she talks about purpose and success she talks about usefulness and other people, to Rolling Stone UK in 2025 and ELLE in 2026 (C14, C14c, C14d, C51g); asked how she knew her talent was special, she said she had never been competitive (C14h), a self-report about talent, not purpose; and her acts at peak moments point outward (C49). Both are weak discriminators.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: The textbook test, what she protects when image and relationship pull apart, is never staged in her public record (C51e). The working discriminator is narrower: what she says the work is for. When she talks about purpose and success she talks about usefulness and other people ("most useful", "to help people, myself included, find compassion and a deeper connection", "how many people you can touch"), in the two interviews where she addressed purpose or success: Rolling Stone UK (2025) and ELLE (2026) (C14, C14c, C14d, C51g). The Apple Music "something to give" line answered how she knew her talent was special and is not counted (C14h, verify-01); asked what she wants next she gives standard standing goals (C07d, C64b). Her outward acts at peaks (C15, C31, C49d, C49e, C29, C30) are consistent with the Two reading but are low-cost and conventional, so they do not discriminate. Against Seven: she holds to the familiar, "I really want to be in my comfort zone" and doubling down on existing musical relationships (C11, C11b). Against Four: she declines to fester and reframes the negative, rejected alt-cool distinction, and hands the songs to listeners (C59, C60, C61). Against Nine: she holds her own agenda firmly, by her own account and her manager's (C35f). Against Six: what she escaped was proving herself, not danger (C10f). The discriminator rests mostly on self-report shaped by an album campaign, so confidence stays medium and Three is named as a close rival.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Her approval independence (deleting the apps, "such peace in that", the 2023 "selfish" defiance; C25, C47, C44) and her insistence on not belonging to anyone (C20, C20e) sit awkwardly with a Two's need to know the giving landed; a Seven or Four streak, therapy, or a feminist stance learned from her mother (C02e, C02b) may explain them better. Her comfort-zone loyalty (C11, C12) reads as Six or Nine security. The goal list and image craft (C07, C26d) are as Three as anything in the record. Her fear of the day she stops having fun or feeling anything while she sings (C23d) is Seven- or Four-flavoured. No family, former-partner or critical testimony exists, so the Two's characteristic costs are not observed (C54). The "selfish" uses differ in tone; only the Carmen remark supports the listener-ownership reading (C40e, C40c).
